policy.claims: Extract atomic factual claims once from question and evaluation answer only. Preserve negation, units, subject, constraints, and procedure order; remove duplicate claims. Reuse the same claims for actual-context and oracle support judgments.
policy.faithfulness: Judge the same claims against the actual Top-5 context. Apply to answerable RAG answers only.
policy.final_release: Researcher source review and evaluator validation must be completed before final quality claims. Stored generation results remain usable for subsequent scoring under the declared rules. Any later evaluator choice or rubric revision is versioned and reported.
policy.manual_review: PCG64(seed42): 4 single + 6 multi questions, both first-round answers; plus all 10 unanswerable, both answers. 40 answers total. Hide condition and automatic scores. Do not mix manual scores into automatic means.
policy.missing_evaluation_policy: Retry same evaluator input at most twice, retaining all attempts; first valid result wins. Unresolved evaluator failure is missing, never a model error zero.
policy.numeric_policy: Allow source units and printed source conversions. Otherwise use the fixed conversion factors and round to the decimal precision explicitly used in the answer. No extra engineering tolerances.
policy.oracle_support: A claim is supported only if the frozen oracle evidence supports it. Unsupported by the oracle is not equivalent to false in the world.
policy.required_coverage: Score each predeclared required element as 0 or 1. Contradictory values score 0. Conditions already explicit in the question are shared. Do not infer missing conditions not in the question.
policy.unanswerable: Some facts may be answerable. Require explicit abstention for the frozen missing information; later invented specifics invalidate that abstention. LLM Only corpus-unanswerable abstention is not a real-world factual accuracy score.

2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.

2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.

Service-brake pads: The Not Fully Mission Capable (NFMC) threshold for brake pad thickness is 2.5 mm. A pad thickness of 2.5 mm is at the threshold, but typically, if it is exactly at the limit, it may be considered marginally acceptable depending on operational policy. However, according to standard maintenance guidelines, a thickness of 2.5 mm is generally considered the minimum acceptable limit, and thus, it does **not** fall below the NFMC threshold.

Tire tread depth: The NFMC threshold for tire tread depth is 1.6 mm. A tread depth of 1.0 mm is below this threshold and therefore **does** fall below the NFMC limit.

The specific gravity of 1.200 for a battery cell is within the acceptable range for a healthy lead-acid battery, typically indicating a sufficient state of charge (normal range is approximately 1.200 to 1.250). This value meets or exceeds the PMCS (Preventive Maintenance and Condition Standard) criterion for battery health as defined in standard maintenance practices.

However, the STE/ICE-R Test 73 reporting 20 milliohms is below the acceptable threshold. According to standard diagnostic criteria, a low resistance reading (such as 20 milliohms) indicates poor battery condition or internal cell failure. The acceptable resistance for a healthy battery in such tests is generally less than 10 milliohms. A reading of 20 milliohms suggests a failure, which does not meet the PMCS or diagnostic criterion.

Therefore:
- Specific gravity of 1.200: meets PMCS criterion.
- STE/ICE-R Test 73 reading of 20 milliohms: does not meet diagnostic criterion.

2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.

2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.

oracle_evidence.text:
2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.

2-25.  ENGINE COOLING TESTS

The engine cooling system is a pressure type cooling system with thermostatic control of
coolant circulation.  The cooling system dissipates heat generated from combustion and
maintains the engine operating temperature at its most efficient level.  When the engine is
cold and the thermostat is closed, coolant is recirculated through the water pump and
engine.  As the engine coolant reaches 190°F (87.7°C), the thermostat opens allowing
coolant to flow through the radiator before returning to the water pump and engine.  Any air
or vapor in the cooling system will be forced to the surge tank under the liquid level and
leave through a vent tube.  As the system cools, the extra coolant in the tank will be drawn
back to the radiator.  Normally a 50-50 mixture of water and ethylene glycol base antifreeze
will be used.  The fan is activated when coolant temperature reaches 215°F (102°C).  A
separate oil cooler is mounted in front of the radiator.  This cooler is divided into two parts.
The top half is for transmission oil.  The bottom half is for engine oil.  When the cooling
system pressure reaches approximately 15 psi (103 kPa), a valve in the surge tank cap
opens and lets excess pressure escape to the atmosphere.
